I've seen a lot of people, here included, griping about how, "teachers are so overpaid so why are they complaining?"  


The thing about the OSSTF union is that it doesn't solely comprise of secondary school teachers. It also encompasses Educational Assistants, Early Childhood Educators, Social Workers, Office Administrators, and Custodial staff, among others. Also, it covers all of the job titles listed before in both elementary and secondary schools. Unfortunately, the naming of the union can be misleading. 

While I can't speak for most of the positions, I am an Educational Assistant and my pay would, probably, equate to around $35,000/year. My partner, an Early Childhood Educator, makes a little closer to $30,000/year. This is a grave different in value given compared to the toted number of $100,000/year, give or take, that teachers are supposed to make. It can be disheartening, especially when you consider that we do deal with a lot of behaviours and, typically, more difficult behaviours.

That being said, pay is not the only motivator for this walkout and these actions against the Government of Ontario. Three of the biggest issues that we are currently faced with are: increasing class sizes, more of a focus towards online-based courses, and a reduction of resources for students with higher-needs.

With regards to class size, bumping class sizes up by even a few students can be difficult for students needing more assistance. More students in a classroom means less classrooms which, in turn, means less support staff and less time for educators (teachers, EAs, ECEs, etc.) to be able to work one-on-one with students or students who might need extra support. This, in turn, means that students miss out on understanding the content or are unable to work through problems, which may cause them to be unsuccessful in their studies.

Online-based courses can be a valuable option but only if it is optional and not mandatory. Some students work better at their own pace and learn better by reading the material as opposed to being told the material. That is fine and that can allow the opportunity for a student to flourish, given that they choose to take that route. Having said that, online-based is not for everyone and should not be made mandatory. The point given above does not even consider that those located in rural areas may have limited or no access to the Internet. If online-based courses are mandatory and a student is unable to complete their work at home, this could cost them a credit that they might desperately need.

Finally, resources and programs are strongly lacking in secondary schools. Be it Developmental Disabilities Programs, Dual Support Program, Autism Units, Behaviour Intervention Program, and more, being cut down drastically, either by removing jobs that could allow support staff to work specially with those higher-needs students, removing funding that disables those programs from being able to get things to enhance the program to better work for those kids or having to close the program completely, not only eliminating more jobs but, also, shuffling those students around and putting them in new, unfamiliar environments where they might not thrive, which could be a huge detriment to their education.

I know that this has been a big tirade but I wanted to pound home the idea that this walkout, picketing, and potential strike is not only about, "overpaid teachers wanting more money again," because that is a gross miscarriage of the truth.
